Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)–based messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics enable in vivo production of diverse protein modalities, but their translation is complicated by multiscale pharmacokinetics encompassing tissue transport, cellular uptake, and intracellular processing.

We developed a platform translational whole-body physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to mechanistically characterize the biodistribution and protein expression of intravenously administered mRNA–LNP therapeutics.

The model integrates receptor-mediated, saturable tissue infiltration, lymphatic recirculation, hepatic uptake, and explicit intracellular processes including endosomal degradation, mRNA escape, translation, and protein turnover.

Parameters were calibrated using comprehensive rat biodistribution data containing both tissue-level mRNA and translated protein measurements, enabling characterization of rapid early tissue deposition and dominant hepatic protein production.

Sensitivity analyses identified endosomal degradation, mRNA stability, and translation efficiency as the primary determinants of hepatic protein exposure, whereas increasing tissue influx alone yielded minimal effect.

Using fundamental allometric scaling principle, the model was translated from rat to human and evaluated against published clinical plasma mRNA pharmacokinetics of an mRNA-encoded monoclonal antibody.
Cell-type specific simulation analyses further demonstrated the competing roles of Kupffer cells and hepatocytes in shaping liver protein exposure.

This whole-body PBPK framework provides a mechanistic and predictive platform to support first-in-human dose selection, to interrogate multilevel determinants of mRNA pharmacokinetics, and to guide rational mRNA-LNP design.

Messenger RNA (mRNA) technology has emerged as a transformative and increasingly established modality in modern therapeutics and vaccine development, offering a versatile platform for targeted protein expression delivered via lipid nanoparticles.
This is exemplified by the unprecedented speed and scale with which mRNA based vaccines were developed against SARS-COV-2 during the COVID-19 pandemic [1, 2].
Similar progress has been achieved with neoantigen mRNA cancer immunotherapy [3, 4], highlighting the versatility of the platform for both infectious disease and oncology vaccine applications.

Beyond applications to vaccine development, the mRNA technology is being explored for therapeutic purposes, such as development of mRNA encoded monoclonal antibodies [5], bispecific antibodies for oncology [6], in situ CAR-T (chimeric antigen receptor T cell) therapy for cancer [7], and mRNA based enzyme replacement therapy for rare diseases [8, 9].

Achieving success in the broader application of lipid-based nanoparticle mRNA (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics requires a quantitative understanding of how LNP based mRNA constructs distribute across tissues, traverse cellular barriers, escape the endosomal pathway and translate into functional protein over clinically relevant dose regimens and time scales.

Unlike other tissue compartments, the liver compartment includes two distinct cell types: Kupffer cells, which are adjacent to the vasculature and directly take up mRNA-LNP from the vasculature, and hepatocytes, that reside within the interstitial space.
Here we report the construction and validation of a whole-body translational PBPK platform for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.
In this modeling framework, pharmacokinetics (PK) refers specifically to mRNA disposition, whereas pharmacodynamics (PD) refers to the resulting encoded protein expression.

Building on the anatomical template of Shah and Betts [15], we introduced Michaelis–Menten infiltration terms to model receptor saturation and receptor mediated tissue infiltration, an endosomal sub-compartment to account for degradation and escape, and mRNA to protein translation within each tissue.
Parameters were calibrated against the comprehensive rat dataset of Ci et al., [22], encompassing both mRNA and translated protein across different organs.

Although the calibration was performed for a specific LNP formulation, the underlying model structure is designed to support re-calibration for other LNP designs, recognizing that differences in chemical composition may alter tissue distribution, cellular uptake, and downstream expression.
The model was then allometrically scaled to human based on fundamental allometric scaling principles.
This allometric scaling was shown to enable adequate prediction of human plasma mRNA PK.

Virtual patient simulations reproduced published plasma PK profiles for an mRNA encoded monoclonal antibody targeting Chikungunya virus at doses from 0.1 to 0.6 mg/kg [5], providing confidence in cross-species scaling.
Following IV injection, mRNA-LNP enters the venous compartment, from which it travels to the rest of the tissues through arterial flow.
From each organ, mRNA-LNP can return to the venous pool via blood flow or enter the lymphatic system through the lymph node, ultimately re-circulating back to the venous compartment.
Within portal organs (small intestine, large intestine, spleen, and pancreas), mRNA-LNP flows into the liver before re-entering the venous circulation.

Quantitative receptor measurements (density, turnover) in relevant vascular beds, time-resolved endosomal pH/escape readouts, and single-cell resolved mRNA/protein trajectories would enable replacement of phenomenological terms with mechanistic modules.
Complementary in vitro studies characterizing species-dependent cellular uptake or endosomal processing would further enhance model validation and mechanistic resolution.
Importantly, application to LNPs with different chemistries or formulations would require appropriate recalibration and validation, which are beyond the scope of the present work.
The rat-scaled model, established based on physiological parameters for a 280-g rat, was calibrated to rat biodistribution data in [22].
The study includes biodistribution data for an intracellular mRNA therapy, in which the translated protein remains within the cell.

Quantified mRNA and protein concentrations across different tissues were measured using a branched DNA (bDNA) assay and an LC-MS/MS assay, respectively, following a 2 mg/kg dose of mRNA administered via 10-minute infusion.
Model calibration steps were as follows: we first calibrated the liver mRNA concentration profile to estimate the tissue influx rate, mRNA degradation rate, and LNP endosomal degradation rate.
Spleen and lung mRNA data were then calibrated by fitting their respective influx rates as well as mRNA and LNP degradation rates.

Ci et al., [22] showed that plasma and liver mRNA concentrations peak within 10–15 min of dosing, a profile incompatible with perfusion-limited tissue uptake.
Sago et al., [23] demonstrated that sub-cellular competition between Kupffer cells, liver endothelial cells, and hepatocytes shape functional delivery of lipid nanoparticles into the liver tissue.
Meanwhile, recent data reveal steep pH-dependent changes in ionizable lipid structure that alter endosomal escape kinetics [24].

Collectively, these findings argue for development of a translational PBPK model that can disentangle early, receptor-driven deposition from downstream intracellular bottlenecks and present an opportunity to predict human mRNA-LNP PK from preclinical species.

Local and global sensitivity analyses consistently suggest an important implication for therapeutic design: hepatic protein exposure is dominated by parameters determining intracellular dynamics of mRNA-LNP, specifically endosomal degradation, mRNA stability, and translation.
Interestingly, liver exposure is less sensitive to increases in LNP tissue influx consistent with previously published modeling results [20].

Increasing mRNA escape from endosomes can linearly tune protein exposure over the explored range, whereas increasing endosomal or mRNA degradation produces strongly nonlinear response with threshold-like behavior.

This result is consistent with available evidence demonstrating the critical role of mRNA stability and escape in modulating the encoded protein exposure, even suggesting mRNA escape as a critical determinant in designing optimal LNP based mRNA therapeutics [31, 32].

These findings are consistent with several well-known empirical levers that could be modulated - ionizable lipid pKa [33] and helper-lipid composition (endosomal escape) [34], UTR/codon design and chemical context (mRNA stability), and 5’ structural elements (translation) [35] - and the PBPK framework could provide a quantitative way to potentially guide the prioritization of which lever will matter most under specific dosing constraints.
We note that the sensitivity analyses were performed at 2 mg/kg dose, where some process may begin to saturate.
Thus, the relative sensitivities should be viewed as dose-dependent and primarily hypothesis generating.

In addition, the model was specifically calibrated to the dataset reported by Ci et al., and further re-calibration and sensitivity analyses would be necessary to assess the relative importance of key mechanistic steps for LNPs with different formulations.

The pharmacokinetics of mRNA-LNP is complex and multi-layered.
Particle size, ionizable-lipid pKa and helper-lipid composition all modulate this corona and hence tissue tropism [12, 13].

Within target organs the particles must cross the endothelial fenestrae, undergo uptake (often via scavenger or LDL-family receptors), survive endosomal degradation and finally release mRNA into the cytosol where ribosomes translate the mRNA into encoded protein.

Consequently, while conventional allometric approaches remain valuable tools, relying on them without accounting for the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) complexities of mRNA-LNP may lead to less informative or potentially misleading dose projections.

For example, if endosomal degradation is a dominant limiter for a given construct, the model predicts pronounced shifts in protein exposure with small changes in escape kinetics—suggesting that modest differences in ionizable lipid composition may manifest as outsized differences in circulating protein (for secreted payloads) or tissue PD (for intracellular targets).

In sum, the platform provides a coherent quantitative scaffold for hypothesis testing, construct prioritization, and FIH planning.

It helps identify which design knobs (lipid chemistry, RNA engineering, dose/infusion) could efficiently impact the clinical exposure and pharmacological response, and it highlights where additional biological characterization will likely offer the greatest return on experimental investment.
